Maine Mayors Coalition Testimony on LD 747, An Act to Provide Funds to Reduce Student Homelessness
Senator Curry, Representative Gere and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Housing and Economic Development, the Maine Mayors Coalition is providing testimony in support of LD 747, An Act to Provide Funds to Reduce Student Homelessness.
The Maine Mayors Coalition is a nonpartisan group representing the mayors of eleven Maine communities - Auburn, Bangor, Biddeford, Lewiston, Portland, Rockland, Saco, Sanford, South Portland, Waterville and Westbrook - and nearly 300,000 residents. The Coalition advocates on behalf of our citizens and municipalities for policies that recognize the vital services Maine cities provide and the positive impact Maine cities have on our state. The Coalition seeks to work in partnership with state and federal elected officials to meet the needs of Maine people.
One of our most important obligations as public officials is to our young people - they are Maine's future. Ensuring they receive a quality education prepares them to become contributing members of society.
As you're well aware, some students face extraordinary challenges in their lives. One such challenge for a growing number of students is not having basic shelter. Over the last few years, municipalities of all sizes have seen more and more students experiencing homelessness.
Among our Coalition members, Lewiston has 420 unhoused students. Auburn reported 234 for the 2023/2024 school year and expects to meet or exceed that number in this school year. Biddeford has 200 unhoused students, South Portland 150, Saco 150 and Westbrook 122. That is close to 1,300 unhoused students in just these six cities. Given fluctuating economic conditions and the state's lack of affordable housing, we expect these numbers will continue to rise, not fall.
We fully support providing unhoused students with rental assistance as proposed in LD 747. It would be much more beneficial - for them, for our cities and for our state - to spend their formative years receiving a quality education instead of worrying about their housing situations.
We ask you to support LD 747 and the funding it would appropriate to Maine State Housing Authority's Rental Assistance Program for Homeless Students. Thank you for your time.

AN ACT TO PROVIDE FUNDS TO REDUCE STUDENT HOMELESSNESS
March 18, 2025
Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and members of the Housing and Economic Development Committee, I am Eileen King, the executive director of the Maine School Superintendents Association, testifying on behalf of the MSSA legislative committee in support of L.D. 747.

VICE PRESIDENT RHONDA SPERREY
RSU 64/MSAD 64 CORINTH, 04427
SECRETARY/TREASURER BENJAMIN SIROIS
VALLEY UNIFIED REGIONAL SERVICE CENTER FORT KENT, 04743
PAST PRESIDENT PATRICIA HOPKINS
MSAD 11 GARDINER, 04345

Over the past two years, the Maine legislature has, for the first time, given our schools important tools to provide critical financial relief to students and families without a permanent place to live each night. Last school year, more than 3,000 students were identified under the McKinney-Vento program. These are Maine's most vulnerable and atrisk students. They are couch-surfing, doubled-up with family or friends, or in temporary hotels or shelters.
For years, Maine schools have worked as hard as possible to assist every student using limited resources. Many have added guidance counselors and social workers who connect students and families with basic services: healthcare, SNAP benefits, or housing assistance. Some communities have gone even further, like in Lewiston, where the school has created "The Store Next Door" as a hub to provide clothing, essentials and other needs for homeless students.

EILEEN E. KING EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR

In 2023, the legislature established a transformative pilot program to allow schools to spend up to $750 per student to keep students housed. This went towards vital needs: utility bills, transportation, basic grocery cards, and more. And the passage of L.D. 1422, last year, was a welcome complement to this work. It paid for housing navigators at schools to work with students and families and even provided rental assistance to students and their families. Schools have never received enough support to truly serve these students, and this assistance was a groundbreaking attempt to make that happen. Together, these policies have ensured educational stability for our most vulnerable students at a time of immense disruption.

49 COMMUNITY DRIVE AUGUSTA ME 04330 (207) 622-3473 (800) 660-8484

We know that housing instability is still just as dire a challenge today for thousands of Maine students and families. Housing prices continue to rise, and more residents struggle to afford the cost-of-living. Our schools are also concerned about potential cuts to federal education funding, which could directly lessen the ability of districts to support at-risk students. The grant program included in this bill would continue to support our students at a crucial moment, and we urge you to support L.D. 747.

Leading for equity, excellence and opportunity for all Maine Students

Good afternoon, Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and Members of the Housing and Economic Development Committee,
My name is Julie Orrego, and I am the Advocacy Supervisor at Preble Street. Preble Street operates 16 programs throughout Maine, and its staff works daily alongside hundreds of individuals and families who struggle with housing insecurity. Our mission is to provide accessible, barrier-free services that empower individuals experiencing challenges related to homelessness, housing, hunger, and poverty and to advocate for solutions to these issues.
Preble Street's Joe Kreisler Teen Shelter is one of only four shelters for homeless youth in Maine. Youth who utilize the Joe Kreisler Teen Shelter connect with caseworkers to meet their basic needs and access other essential services, such as healthcare, employment, housing, and education. Every day, we see the challenges that students experiencing homelessness or housing insecurity face, like moving from one school district to another, living in unsafe conditions, or dealing with unstable family situations. LD747 - An Act to Provide Funds to Reduce Student Homelessness would continue funding a rental assistance program for homeless students in both primary and secondary schools in Maine, making it easier for these students to access stable housing.
The 2024 Point in Time Count found that 19.5% of all households experiencing homelessness had at least one child under 18. According to the Maine State Housing Authority, over eleven proposals totaling almost $5 million in funding requests were submitted by school districts. These numbers indicate the need to make this program permanent.
Preble Street supports LD747 because it helps ensure that every student can succeed academically, regardless of their housing status. When a student is unhoused, they are balancing a number of academic as well as normative youth development issues. By remedying the housing portion of this equation, this bill would provide critical additional resources and support to help students succeed.
Preble Street encourages you to support this legislation because it invests in a brighter future for young people in our state. Every student deserves the opportunity to reach their full potential without their socioeconomic status holding them back.
Thank you for your consideration.

50 years of turning hunger and homelessness into opportunity and hope

Testimony of Representative Michael Brennan presenting
LD 747, An Act to Provide Funds to Reduce Student Homelessness
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Housing and Economic Development
Good afternoon, Senator Curry, Representative Gere and distinguished members of the Joint
Standing Committee on Housing and Economic Development. My name is Michael Brennan,
and I represent House District 115, which includes a portion of Portland.
Today, I am here to introduce LD 747, An Act to Provide Funds to Reduce Student
Homelessness. This bill continues the program and funding approved last year by this committee and
Legislature.
At this point, the effort has gotten off to an excellent start and the potential impact is very promising (see report). The need for this program has been further demonstrated by a recent report from the Maine Education Policy Research Institute (MEPRI) that showed the high school graduation rate for homeless students was 59%, compared to an overall rate of 86%.
Also, this bill changes the name of the subsidy program for homeless students to the "rental
assistance program for homeless students."
According to the Maine Department of Education, 5,223 students were homeless or experienced some kind of housing insecurity in 2023. This committee knows well the ramifications for unhoused children -- from poor health and developmental delays to school instability to increased risk of victimization. This funding is crucial to help the most vulnerable children at the earliest
stages possible.
Thank you for your time and consideration. I am happy to answer any questions.

January 16, 2025

MaineHousing awarded $2 million to fund pilot programs aimed at preventing student homelessness in five school systems, including Portland's, the agency announced.

School systems in Portland, Lewiston, Biddeford, Bath and rural Aroostook County will use
the money to hire housing and homelessness prevention specialists. The systems can also use the money to provide direct financial relief to keep homeless and students in unstable situations in their homes or to secure new housing, the agency said in a written statement
Wednesday.

The pilot program is designed to be flexible "to best meet the needs of the family needing

Derek Davis/Portland Press Herald, file

help," Lauren Bustard, senior director of

homeless initiatives at MaineHousing, said in a written statement.

Roughly 1,700 students and their families are expected to benefit from the pilot, the agency
said.

Portland received the largest grant of just over $759,000, which should help an estimated 650 students, the agency said.

Bath got roughly $442,000 to help 300 students; Aroostook County roughly $353,000 to help 110 students; Biddeford and York County got $275,000 to help 200 students; and Lewiston was awarded roughly $169,000 to help between 400 and 500 students, the agency said.

The awardees were selected from 11 proposals, totaling nearly $5 million in requested funds, MaineHousing said. The money comes from a one-time source of funding approved by Gov. Janet Mills and the state Legislature.

"Unfortunately, demand for these valuable state resources far outstripped the available funds," MaineHousing director Dan Brennan said in a written statement. "As with all pilot
programs, we look forward to learning all we can - in this case, to better prevent
homelessness for students in the future."

MAINE SERVICE CENTERS COALITION
60 Community Drive  Augusta, Maine 04330  (207) 623-8428
Testimony of the Maine Service Centers Coalition LD 747, An Act to Provide Funds to Reduce Student Homelessness
Senator Curry, Representative Gere and esteemed members of the Joint Standing Committee on Housing and Economic Development, the Maine Service Centers Coalition is submitting testimony in support of LD 747, An Act to Provide Funds to Reduce Student Homelessness.
The Maine Service Centers Coalition, comprised of 26 towns and cities across the state, articulates the importance of healthy and thriving service center communities, advocates for public policy that supports and contributes to the economic and social viability of our communities, and collaborates with municipal officials, legislators, state agencies and nonprofits to pursue quality of life for all who live and work in our state.
As you well know, homelessness continues to be a serious issue across our state. Our service center communities are acutely aware of its impact with so many individuals and families turning to our cities and towns in search of housing. We are especially concerned about the growing number of students in our schools who are experiencing homelessness.
Young people are Maine's greatest asset. It is up to all of us to provide them with the best education possible so they have the opportunity to become thriving members of our communities and our state. Sadly, for more and more young people, their ability to learn is being impeded by their lack of basic shelter.
LD 747 would allocate $2 million in both years of the next biennium to the Maine State Housing Authority to "provide rental assistance directly to homeless students or to an adult family member or guardian of the homeless student." Access to these funds would offer housing stability to many of the unhoused students we are seeing in our schools, giving them the security to focus on their studies rather than where they will be sleeping at night. The impacts would be significant and long lasting for our students whose lives have been upended by homelessness.
Please give every consideration to supporting LD 747. It is a worthwhile investment in Maine's young people as well as in the future of our state.
Thank you for your time and attention to this important housing and education issue.

MAINE COUNCIL OF SCHOOL BOARD ATTORNEYS
Isabel Ekman, Esq., Chair

TESTIMONY IN OPPOSITION TO
L.D. 747
AN ACT TO PROVIDE FUNDS TO REDUCE STUDENT HOMELESSNESS
March 18, 2025
Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and members of the Housing and Economic Development Committee, I am Steven Bailey, the executive director of the Maine School Boards Association, speaking on behalf of the MSBA Legislative Committee in opposition to L.D. 747.
This was a difficult decision for our association, as school board members believe in supporting the academic and social needs of all of our students. This is a deep, longstanding value and is in fact included in our organization's System of Resolutions:
"The Maine School Boards Association recognizes that there are many social needs of children that affect leaning. Therefore, local boards are encouraged to examine the role of their schools in meeting the needs of students and their families in a coordinated manner."
School boards take this responsibility seriously. Many districts are prioritizing the addition of social workers to directly work with these students and get them the supports they need. Schools throughout Maine also work together with nonprofits and municipal officials to connect families with General Assistance and other local resources.
If our state budget was in a better situation, we would likely voice our full support for L.D. 747, but that is not the case.
As you all know, our state faces a challenging budget situation over the next biennium. At the same time, school board members are deeply concerned about proposed cuts to education on the federal level, which we worry could lead to the loss of potentially millions of dollars to Maine schools. We expect our state and local governments may need to make up the difference or risk losing programming.
In this environment, our school board members believe that legislators should prioritize existing educational priorities - 55% state funding, support for students with disabilities, universal school meals - and should not consider additional costs that could jeopardize our core priorities. Unfortunately, because of this difficult environment, we would ask you to vote "ought not to pass" on L.D. 747.
